newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua gives go-ahead to 'dry canal' study.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua gives go-ahead to 'dry canal' study.

text.p: The Nicaraguan government on Tuesday cleared the way to begin a feasibility study for the construction of a proposed "dry canal" across Nicaragua that would complement the Panama Canal.

"The formal feasibility studies will begin within the next few months and will take about one year. If all goes well, and the project is approved, we expect to begin construction in January 1998," Don Bosco, president of Canal Interoceanico de Nicaragua S.A. (CINN), told Reuters.

A government-appointed commission will analyse the results of the study and if the commission approves it will recommend that the government award the canal concession to CINN, a private consortium that has major construction and shipping interests from the U.S., Europe and Asia as informal partners.

The $1.5 billion mega-project, the largest in Nicaraguan history, involves the construction of a 220-mile (350 km) high- speed rail link to transport container cargo across the Central American isthmus.
The project also includes construction of two deep-water container ports connected by the rail link and will deal exclusively in container cargo, CINN general manager Juan Carlos Rivas said.
If the study is approved and construction goes as planned, the dry canal would be operational in five or six years, said Pablo Vijil, Nicaragua's minister of construction and transportation.
Crossing Central America on the dry canal would take four to five hours and the rates would be cheaper than the Panama Canal's, Vijil said.
The project is expected to create 20,000 direct jobs and 70,000 spin-off jobs in Nicaragua, one of the poorest countries in Latin America, and would lead to a boom in foreign investment, Vijil said.
Similar canal projects have been proposed for Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Colombia and Costa Rica.

"We chose Nicaragua because we feel the political conditions here have matured, and its topography and deep-water ports give Nicaragua the best position in all of Central America for a project of this kind," Bosco said.
Vijil said Nicaragua now has a step up on the competition and its government has been more receptive to the idea than neighbouring governments.
The dry canal would complement the Panama Canal and not compete with it, since container cargo represents a small minority of the traffic through the Panama Canal, Rivas said.
